newsitem.title: CHINA: China interbank debt trading hit by oversupply.
newsitem.headline: China interbank debt trading hit by oversupply.

text.p: China's new interbank state debt trading has been plagued by heavy oversupply of funds and a lack of borrowers, and this could keep the market dull for a long time, analysts said on Thursday.
"There is huge money supply among banks and few need to borrow from the market," said one banker, who trades the interbank on the market.

"The central government has yet to set up mechanisms to allow the market to have enough borrowers, but because this is a time-consuming process, interbank state debt trading will remain very dull for the foreseeable future," she said.

The People's Bank of China, the central bank, ordered state banks in early June to stop trading state debt on the Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges and regional debt trading centres and to move their trading to the local currency interbank market.

China's state banks used to lend short-term money to securities houses, trust firms and financial firms associated with major industrial companies by trading state debt repurchase contracts on the exchanges and the local debt trading centres, analysts said.

After the central bank ordered them to trade state debt separately on the interbank market -- a mesure aimed at taking bank money out of the volatile stock markets -- the banks lost their major borrowers, the analysts said.
The borrowers included financial firms that had yet to be allowed to trade on the market, they said.
The state banks began trading on the interbank market on June 16 and the average daily turnover has only been around 350 million yuan ($43 million) since then, exchange figures show.
This compares with a daily trading turnover of around four billion yuan in state debt contracts on the Shanghai stock exchange, traded by brokerages, trust and industrial firms.

Interest rates for state debt repurchase contracts had been lower on average against the rates on the exchanges and regional trading centres and had moved in a very narrow range due to weak demand, traders said.
"Interbank state trading is now a unilateral market," said an investment analyst with a major Chinese brokerage.
"With only banks on the market, the problem of oversupply is very serious.
"It needs to be expanded quickly with the admission of new members, including those financial firms associated with the industrial groups," he said.
"One way of helping to activate interbank bank state debt trading is for the central bank to quickly expand its open market operations," said another analyst.

The People's Bank started its open market operations in April last year, trading short-term debt with the banks to help control money supply in China and using the operations as a way to indicate central monetary policy.
However, volume has been very thin and the operations are officially considered to be still on trial.

The official China Securities newspaper said on Wednesday that the process of moving state banks' state debt positions to the newly established central state debt depository was part of the reason for dull debt trading on the interbank market.

China set up the Beijing-based depository, the China Government Securities Depository Trust and Clearing Co, in February to co-ordinate all debt trading and to hold, clear and settle all state debt transactions.
